1.note: Based on the previous chapter, the Israelites might have **set out** from Bashan. However, Numbers 33:48 indicates that the Israelites traveled to **the plains of Moab** from the mountains of Abarim. It is possible that the previous chapter describes the movements of the army, not the rest of the Israelites. It is also possible that Numbers 33 does not include all the places where the Israelites stopped. So, it is recommended that you do not explicitly indicate where the Israelites **set out** from in this verse. Alternate translation: [And the sons of Israel moved on] or [The Israelites continued to walk]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Israel]
The author is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

2.note: Here the author is introducing **Balak the son of Zippor** as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [There was a man named Balak the son of Zippor, and he]

3.q: וַ⁠יָּ֨גָר מוֹאָ֜ב מִ⁠פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠עָ֛ם מְאֹ֖ד כִּ֣י רַב־ה֑וּא
3.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because the people were many, Moab was very afraid from the face of the people.]

Here, **Moab** represents the people of Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the people of Moab were very afraid]

The author is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on account of the people]
See how you translated the similar expression in [22:1](ta:22).

4.note: The author is using **Moab** to represent the king and leaders of Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the leaders of Moab said to the elders of Midian]

Moab is using **will lick up all around us** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [will consume everything around us]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the ox licks up the greenery of the field**, consuming it entirely, so the assembly of Israel will consume everything around Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [leaving nothing, just as an ox eats up all the greenery of a field]

4.q: וּ⁠בָלָ֧ק בֶּן־צִפּ֛וֹר מֶ֥לֶךְ לְ⁠מוֹאָ֖ב בָּ⁠עֵ֥ת הַ⁠הִֽוא
4.note: Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

5.note: Here, the phrase **to call for him** marks the purpose for which Balak sent the messengers to Balaam. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.
The pronoun **he** refers to Balak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Balak sent messengers]

Here the author is introducing **Balaam the son of Beor** as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [to a man named Balaam, the son of Beor]

The implication is that **the River** here refers to the Euphrates River. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the great Euphrates River]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [the people of his own descent]

The phrase **his people** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading that some scholars have suggested. Alternate translation: [the sons of Amaw]
The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated **saying** in [1:1](ta:01).

Here Balak is speaking as if the surface of the land were an **eye**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it has covered the surface of the land]

5.q: כִסָּה֙ & עֵ֣ין הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ וְ⁠ה֥וּא יֹשֵׁ֖ב מִ⁠מֻּלִֽ⁠י
5.note: The pronoun it refers to the people who had come out from Egypt. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [that people has covered the eye of the land, and that people is dwelling in front of me]

6.q: וְ⁠עַתָּה֩ לְכָ⁠ה־נָּ֨א אָֽרָ⁠ה־לִּ֜⁠י אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֗ה כִּֽי־עָצ֥וּם הוּא֙ מִמֶּ֔⁠נִּי
6.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And now, because this people is mightier than I, please come, curse it for me]

The words translated as **come** and **curse** are imperatives, but they communicate a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [I ask that you come and curse this people for me]

The expression **blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God blesses]

The expression **cursed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God curses]

7.note: Here, **their hand** represents what they were carrying with them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [carrying divinations with them]

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The term **divinations** refers to payments given to someone in exchange for practicing divination, the attempt to gain hidden knowledge through magical or occult means. If your readers would not be familiar with what divinations are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [payments for divining]

8.note: The phrase **the princes of Moab** refers to the same men whom the author called “the elders of Moab” in the previous verse. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could make this clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [these same leaders of Moab]

9.note: God is using the question form to prompt Balaam to tell him about his visitors, not because he does not know. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Tell me about these men who are with you.]

10.q: בָּלָ֧ק בֶּן־צִפֹּ֛ר מֶ֥לֶךְ מוֹאָ֖ב שָׁלַ֥ח אֵלָֽ⁠י & הִנֵּ֤ה הָ⁠עָם֙ הַ⁠יֹּצֵ֣א מִ⁠מִּצְרַ֔יִם וַ⁠יְכַ֖ס אֶת־עֵ֣ין הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ עַתָּ֗ה לְכָ֤⁠ה קָֽבָ⁠ה־לִּ⁠י֙ אֹת֔⁠וֹ אוּלַ֥י אוּכַ֛ל לְ⁠הִלָּ֥חֶם בּ֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠גֵרַשְׁתִּֽי⁠ו
10.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Balak the son of Zippor, the king of Moab, sent word to me that the people coming out from Egypt have covered the eye of the land. He asked me to come and curse that people for him so that he may perhaps be able to fight against that people and drive it out.]

10.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֥אמֶר בִּלְעָ֖ם אֶל־הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֑ים בָּלָ֧ק בֶּן־צִפֹּ֛ר מֶ֥לֶךְ מוֹאָ֖ב שָׁלַ֥ח אֵלָֽ⁠י
10.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. It may be more natural to express this whole statement as an indirect quotation, as modeled by the UST. Alternate translation: [And Balaam told God that Balak the son of Zippor, the king of Moab, had sent to him]

11.note: See how you translated these same phrases in Numbers 22:5. Alternate translation: [it has covered the surface of the land]
See how you translated these same phrases in Numbers 22:6. Alternate translation: [I ask that you come and curse it for me]

11.q: וַ⁠יְכַ֖ס אֶת־עֵ֣ין הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ עַתָּ֗ה לְכָ֤⁠ה קָֽבָ⁠ה־לִּ⁠י֙ אֹת֔⁠וֹ אוּלַ֥י אוּכַ֛ל לְ⁠הִלָּ֥חֶם בּ֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠גֵרַשְׁתִּֽי⁠ו
11.note: The pronoun **it** refers to the people coming out from Egypt. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and they have covered the eye of the land. Now come, curse them for me. Perhaps I will be able to fight against them and drive them out]

12.note: The expression **blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [I have blessed it]

13.q: וַ⁠יָּ֤קָם בִּלְעָם֙ בַּ⁠בֹּ֔קֶר וַ⁠יֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל־שָׂרֵ֣י בָלָ֔ק לְכ֖וּ אֶֽל־אַרְצְ⁠כֶ֑ם כִּ֚י מֵאֵ֣ן יְהוָ֔ה לְ⁠תִתִּ֖⁠י לַ⁠הֲלֹ֥ךְ עִמָּ⁠כֶֽם
13.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And Balaam rose in the morning and said to the princes of Balak, “Because Yahweh has refused to give me to go with you, go to your land.”]

15.note: Balak is using **added again** as a common expression of the culture to mean “did something again.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Balak again sent princes] or [Balak sent more princes]
The pronoun **these** refers to the princes whom Balak sent the first time. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [than the princes he had sent the first time]

16.q: כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ בָּלָ֣ק בֶּן־צִפּ֔וֹר אַל־נָ֥א תִמָּנַ֖ע מֵ⁠הֲלֹ֥ךְ אֵלָֽ⁠י
16.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Balak the son of Zippor says that you should not let anything keep you from coming to him]

The expression **be withheld** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [do not allow anything to hold you back]

17.note: Balak is repeating forms of the verb **honor** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I will surely honor you]
See how you translated these same phrases in Numbers 22:6. Alternate translation: [I ask that you come and curse this people for me]

18.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fullness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [everything that fills his house]

Balaam is using **the mouth of Yahweh my God** to represent what Yahweh commands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the command of Yahweh my God]

Balaam is referring to any action at all by naming two extremes, **small** and **great**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to do anything at all]

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [to do anything, whether small or great]

19.note: Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [dwell in this place tonight]

20.note: God is speaking as if this were a hypothetical possibility, but he means that it is actually true. If your language does not state something as a condition if it is certain or true, or if your readers might think that what God is saying is uncertain, then you could translate this as a confident statement. Alternate translation: [Since the men have come to call for you]

20.q: וְ⁠אַ֗ךְ & הַ⁠דָּבָ֛ר אֲשֶׁר־אֲדַבֵּ֥ר אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ אֹת֥⁠וֹ תַעֲשֶֽׂה
20.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the phrase **it you shall do** with or before the phrase **the word that I speak to you**. Alternate translation: [But you shall do only the word that I speak to you]

21.note: The author is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

22.note: The author is using the phrase **the nose of God burned** as a common expression of the culture to mean that God is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God became angry]
The pronoun **he** refers to Balaam. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [because Balaam was going]

The author is introducing **the angel of Yahweh** as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Now there was an angel of Yahweh who stationed himself]

22.q: וְ⁠הוּא֙ רֹכֵ֣ב עַל־אֲתֹנ֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁנֵ֥י נְעָרָ֖י⁠ו עִמּֽ⁠וֹ
22.note: Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Here, the phrase **two of his young men** could imply: (1) that Balaam had more than these two servants, but these two went with him. Alternate translation: [two young men from his household] (2) that Balaam had only these two servants. Alternate translation: [and his two young men]

23.note: The expression **being drawn** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he had drawn his sword in his hand]
Here, the phrase **to turn her aside to the way** marks the purpose for which Balaam struck the donkey. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

24.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [with a wall on this side and a wall on that side]

25.note: The pronoun **she** refers to the female donkey. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the donkey pressed herself]

The author is using **added to strike** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam struck the donkey again, that is, an additional time. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he hit her once more] or [he hit her again]

26.note: The author is using **added to pass over** as a common expression of the culture to mean “continued traveling onward.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [continued on ahead] or [kept going]

27.note: The author is using the phrase **the nose of Balaam burned** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Balaam became furious]

28.q: מֶה־עָשִׂ֣יתִֽי לְ⁠ךָ֔ כִּ֣י הִכִּיתַ֔⁠נִי זֶ֖ה שָׁלֹ֥שׁ רְגָלִֽים
28.note: The donkey is using the question form to protest what Balaam has done, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I have done nothing to you that should make you strike me these three times!]

29.q: ל֤וּ יֶשׁ־חֶ֨רֶב֙ בְּ⁠יָדִ֔⁠י כִּ֥י & עַתָּ֖ה הֲרַגְתִּֽי⁠ךְ
29.note: Balaam is making a conditional statement that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. He is stating it as a condition to show that killing the donkey is not possible for him. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: [I wish I had a sword in my hand, because then I would kill you now]

30.q: הֲ⁠לוֹא֩ אָנֹכִ֨י אֲתֹֽנְ⁠ךָ֜ אֲשֶׁר־רָכַ֣בְתָּ עָלַ֗⁠י מֵ⁠עֽוֹדְ⁠ךָ֙ עַד־הַ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה
30.note: The donkey is using the question form to remind Balaam of their long relationship, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I am your female donkey on which you have ridden from since you were until this day.]

The donkey is using **from since you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “from the time you first owned me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the time you first owned me]

The donkey is using the question form to insist that it has never behaved this way before, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I have never been accustomed to do thus to you!]

31.note: Here the author is speaking as if Balaam’s inability to see the angel had been a covering over his **eyes** that Yahweh removed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh enabled Balaam to see]

The terms **bowed** and **prostrated himself** mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [And he bowed low]

The author is using the phrase **prostrated himself to his nostrils** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam lay face-down on the ground. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and lay face-down on the ground]

32.q: מָ֗ה הִכִּ֨יתָ֙ & אֲתֹ֣נְ⁠ךָ֔ זֶ֖ה שָׁל֣וֹשׁ רְגָלִ֑ים
32.note: The angel of Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke Balaam, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not have struck your female donkey these three times]

Here the angel is speaking of Balaam’s course of action as if it were a **way** or road that is steep and dangerous. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your course of action is reckless before me]

33.q: אוּלַי֙ נָטְתָ֣ה מִ⁠פָּנַ֔⁠י כִּ֥י עַתָּ֛ה גַּם־אֹתְ⁠כָ֥ה הָרַ֖גְתִּי & הֶחֱיֵֽיתִי
33.note: The angel says **Unless she turned aside from my face** to introduce an imaginary situation, describing what would have happened if the donkey had not turned away. Use a natural method in your language for introducing an imaginary situation. Alternate translation: [If she had not turned away from my face, then by now I would have killed you and let her live]

Here, **my face** represents the angel’s presence, that is, being in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [she turned aside from my presence]

34.q: חָטָ֔אתִי כִּ֚י לֹ֣א יָדַ֔עְתִּי כִּ֥י אַתָּ֛ה נִצָּ֥ב לִ⁠קְרָאתִ֖⁠י בַּ⁠דָּ֑רֶךְ
34.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [“Because I did not know that you were being stationed to meet me in the way, I have sinned.”]

Balaam is using **in your eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in your judgment” or “in your opinion.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [if in your judgment {it is} evil]

Balaam is describing a possible situation in which he would return home if his going on this journey displeases the angel of Yahweh. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Suppose my going is evil in your eyes. Then let me return for myself]

35.q: וְ⁠אֶ֗פֶס & הַ⁠דָּבָ֛ר אֲשֶׁר־אֲדַבֵּ֥ר אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ אֹת֣⁠וֹ תְדַבֵּ֑ר
35.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the phrase **it you shall speak** with or before the phrase **the word that I speak to you**. Alternate translation: [but you shall speak only the word that I speak to you]

36.note: The author is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

Here, the phrase **the city of Moab** could be: (1) a reference to a specific city in Moab, which is identified by the following phrases. Alternate translation: [a specific city in Moab] (2) the name “Ir Moab.” Alternate translation: [Ir Moab]
The word **Arnon** is the name of a river.

37.q: הֲ⁠לֹא֩ שָׁלֹ֨חַ שָׁלַ֤חְתִּי אֵלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ לִ⁠קְרֹא־לָ֔⁠ךְ לָ֥⁠מָּה לֹא־הָלַ֖כְתָּ אֵלָ֑⁠י הַֽ⁠אֻמְנָ֔ם לֹ֥א אוּכַ֖ל כַּבְּדֶֽ⁠ךָ
37.note: Balak is using the question form three times for emphasis, not to ask for information. In the first question, he stresses that he had indeed summoned Balaam; in the second, he rebukes Balaam for not coming sooner; and in the third, he asserts that he is certainly able to reward Balaam. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for those purposes, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [I certainly sent to you to call for you! You should have come to me immediately! I am truly able to honor you!]

38.note: Balaam is using the question form to stress that he cannot say whatever he wants, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I am certainly not able to say anything on my own!]

Here Balaam is speaking as if the message that God wants him to speak were an object that God **puts** into his mouth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The message that God gives me to say] or [The words that God wants me to say]
